title: Latent Journey — sparring notes on tiered UX for variable-response products
content:
Context:
This is a personal sprint-of-thoughts doc exploring a UX pattern for letting apps expose variable-response 'lanes' to end users (and dev teams) — basically thinking about how customers might choose or default between compact/fast answers, contextual-rich answers, and explanation-first answers. Goal is to surface a lightweight UI + API contract that maps to Redwood inference runtime features (batching/caching, quant profiles, model variants, and fallback routing).

Problem statement:
- Customers often ask for both 'cheap' and 'high-fidelity' outputs from the same assistant (one for quick lookups, one for evaluations/final content).
- Current approach (multiple endpoints + feature flags) is heavy. Need a small surface area for product teams to expose tiers without proliferating routes.
- UX must make cost/latency trade-offs visible when it matters, but not overwhelming.

Key ideas (brainstorm):
1) Response Lanes (visual metaphor): three visible lanes in the assistant UI: "Snap", "Balanced", "Deep". Each lane maps to a profile: snapshot (low-token, shallow decoding, quantized small model), balanced (default medium), deep (long context, higher temperature/ensemble, optionally GPU-dedicated).
   - Lanes are presets; client can override per-request.
   - Show small tag under reply: e.g., "Snap — 80ms, ~3¢" (approximate cost/latency).

2) Latent Journey visualization: a compact timeline that shows how the same conversation would have answered across lanes. Minimal UI: a toggle for "compare lanes" that shows 2–3-line diffs. Useful in settings where user wants to 'upgrade' a response.

3) Upgrade/Replay flow: user sees a Snap answer, clicks "upgrade" -> triggers re-gen on "Deep" with same constraints and links to previous. System should show delta tokens used and allow rollback.

4) Developer API contract: one route POST /responses with body: {prompt, lane: "snap|balanced|deep", budget_hard?: token_limit, fidelity_profile?: "clarity|creativity", session_id?}. Server-side maps lane to model variant + quant + routing policy.

5) Cost transparency: surface an estimate pre-send (small tooltip) and post-response actual token count. Allow orgs to hide cost in user-facing UI but keep in console.

User stories:
- As a product manager, I want an option to let power users request 'High fidelity' so they can re-run any assistant reply for export-quality edits.
- As an end user, I want a fast answer most of the time, but when I need subtleties, I can request a deeper explanation without losing conversation state.
- As an ML engineer, I want routing to fall back gracefully: if Deep is saturated, route to Balanced and indicate a degraded lane in the upgrade flow.

Acceptance criteria (v0):
- Single API route supports lane selector, defaulting to Balanced.
- Console shows per-request token and latency metrics broken down by lane.
- Client SDK includes small helper for preflight cost estimate.
- Upgrade flow exists as backend endpoint that replays request under different lane and returns diffs + cost.

Open questions / risks:
- Billing model: should lane upgrades be billed as separate calls (likely yes) — needs clarity with billing/invoicing.
- Privacy/regulatory: Deep lane might enable longer context caching; ensure retention rules applied per org.
- UX friction: too many lanes confuse users; need simple defaults and progressive disclosure.

Experiment matrix (quick):
- Metric: % of sessions that use upgrade flow; cost delta per session; NPS for power users on quality.
- Variants: 2-lane (Snap/Balanced) vs 3-lane (Snap/Balanced/Deep). Measure upgrade frequency and average tokens consumed.

Implementation sketch (infra hooks):
- Route mapping table (config in control plane): lane -> {model_family, quant_profile, priority_pool, token_budget_default, cache_policy}
- Runtime should expose a lightweight preflight: simulate token estimate + predict latency based on current queue lengths (for UI tooltip).
- Upgrade should carry session KV cache snapshot id so Deep can warm based on what Snap produced (to avoid cold-start cost).

Short UI wire notes (for FE):
- Minimal bottom bar with lane pill and cost estimate.
- Reply card includes a micro-CTA: "Upgrade for more detail" with expected incremental cost.
- Compare toggle opens a small side-by-side overlay (first 2 replies only).

Implementation TODOs (me):
- [ ] Draft API proto for lane selector + upgrade endpoint (Linear: create ticket INF-712)
- [ ] Light console mockups for lane metrics and cost breakdown (ask Drew to prototype)
- [ ] Quick backend mapping POC: Balanced->gptx-medium-8q, Deep->gptx-large-4q-dedicated, Snap->gptx-small-4q
- [ ] Security review note: include retention flags in request, default to org policy.

Notes-to-self / scribbles:
- Could pair lane selector with session presets (e.g., "research mode") that persist across a session.
- Consider throttles: upgrades limited per session or per-org to prevent cost spikes.
- Think about auto-upgrade heuristics: detect user signal ("this looks wrong") and suggest upgrade.

References / links:
- Existing session presets doc: /shared_drives/product/session-ontology-exploratory-notes (link to Confluence TBD)
- Related ticket: INF-402 (fallback routing improvements)
- Slack thread: #product-research "lane idea" (pings: @mika)

Bottom line: aim for an MVP that is easy to adopt (small API change + client helper) and surfaces clear upgrade UX so users can choose fidelity without fragmenting endpoints. This doc is a living scratchpad — will refine after quick mock and infra sanity check.
